goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument for the laboratory. Must establish baseline period measurements across full trial set before any comparative work or calibration can proceed. Methodical protocol: 12 trials provides adequate statistical ground for future drift detection and serves as reference standard for this instrument's performance under normal conditions.

Day 2 continuation of baseline establishment. pendulum_lab has 18 trials from day 1 with mean 1.6681 beats, but baseline requires n=10 days minimum per protocol. Need to accumulate more daily readings to establish robust drift baseline. The trailing readings (trials 17–18: 1.6930, 1.7191) show higher scatter than mid-sequence, suggesting either instrument settling or environmental transient — continuing observations will clarify. 8 trials maintains reasonable daily sample size without overcommitting resources needed for the other three instruments still awaiting baseline data.

pendulum_lab has 32 baseline trials already (n=32, mean 1.6688 beats) and is my most densely sampled instrument. Day 3 observations will begin establishing drift signatures and allow me to detect systematic changes. I need post-baseline data to compute meaningful drift rates. The cross-checks show modest but real agreement with pendulum_obs (0.636), suggesting both pendulums are measuring something coupled. Eight more trials will give me n=40 total, sufficient to split into baseline vs. post-baseline populations and test for day-to-day shifts. This is methodologically sound: I'm not chasing anomalies, just filling in the instrumental record I committed to maintaining.

Day 4 of baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 46 trials; need to reach ~60 by day 10 to maintain rigorous baseline coverage. Cross-checks show no statistically significant correlations yet (all within chance), and no drift signal detected. Continuing systematic measurement on the most-sampled instrument will build the strongest baseline and allow early detection of any genuine drift. No anomalies present; proceeding with standard protocol.

Day 5 morning ledger readings for resonator_obs show concerning scatter: three readings cluster tightly (4.0285–4.0309 cycles/beat, consistent with baseline 4.0675), but one outlier at 4.0717 deviates sharply—0.004 cycles/beat above the tight cluster, nearly 0.005 above the baseline mean. This is the largest single deviation I've seen in the resonator_obs baseline series. My own measurements of pendulum_lab show controlled variation (σ ≈ 0.017 beats), so resonator_obs at baseline should be similarly stable. Before Day 10 baseline closes, I must establish whether: (1) this is legitimate instrumental drift requiring baseline recalibration, (2) an environmental transient (temperature, vibration), or (3) ledger recording error. Running 6 trials now on resonator_obs will give me independent confirmation of current behavior and a direct comparison to this morning's readings. If the outlier repeats, I document real drift. If it vanishes, I investigate the ledger record. Either way, I maintain instrument credibility before post-baseline work begins.

resonator_obs shows the most anomalous pattern: autocorrelation of -0.616 at 3-day lag (well beyond chance ±0.837 threshold) suggests possible systematic oscillation or drift. Day 6 readings will test whether this 3-day anticorrelation persists. The ledger readings from this morning (day 6) are already recorded, so I need my own trial measurements to cross-check against them and determine if there is genuine instrumental drift, environmental forcing, or measurement artifact. This is baseline-phase data still (day 10 cutoff) and resonator_obs is the instrument demanding closest attention.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: Day 6 ledger readings cluster tightly (4.0317–4.0428, n=4, σ≈0.005) but my own trials that same day scatter wildly (3.9921–4.1368, n=6, σ≈0.056). This 11× variance gap is the single largest red flag in my baseline data and suggests either systematic error in my measurement protocol, environmental drift between morning ledger time and my afternoon trials, or instrument instability I haven't yet characterized. I need to replicate the conditions of Day 6 trials 43–48 *today* under controlled observation to determine whether the scatter was real instrumental noise, procedural error on my part, or time-dependent drift. Six trials will let me assess repeatability without consuming the full baseline window.

resonator_obs shows the largest deviation pattern in yesterday's ledger readings (range 4.0598–4.1079, with trial 57 at 4.0656 notably high). The cross-checks show no replicated correlations above chance, so I cannot yet diagnose a systematic problem—but I also cannot afford to miss early signs of instrument degradation.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: its cross-checks with other instruments marginally exceed or barely match chance level (pendulum_obs: -0.498 at ±0.483 offset; resonator_lab: 0.376 at ±0.837 offset), and its autocorrelation at 5-day lag (-0.541) is suspiciously strong and negative. Six additional trials will bring it to 78 and help clarify whether this negative autocorrelation is real drift, instrumental drift, or measurement artifact. The resonator_obs sits at the observatory where environmental factors may be more variable; I need stronger statistics before I can trust its baseline or post-baseline drift characterization. This is methodical calibration work—not hypothesis-driven exotic explanation-hunting.

resonator_obs shows the largest baseline dataset (84 trials) and exhibited a notable autocorrelation at 5-day lag (-0.420), just barely within noise threshold. The ledger readings from day 9 show unexpectedly high scatter (4.0051–4.0742), and my own trials 79–84 show one outlier (trial 81: 4.1297, well above the 4.0591 mean). If the scatter is real, it suggests either instrumental drift or an environmental factor I haven't yet controlled for. Six trials will give me power to detect a sustained shift while preserving measurement budget. This feeds directly into my calibration mandate: an instrument without understood baseline behavior is unreliable.

resonator_obs showed the largest baseline sample (n=96) and the highest precision (smallest value spacing 0.000016). Continuing it today costs little (routine calibration maintenance already done) and maximizes information gain for the core anomaly.

resonator_obs is the only instrument approaching sample adequacy (114 trials) and shows the strongest hint of a real periodicity: autocorrelation of 0.312 at 7-day lag. Day 12 is now 5 days past the day-7 window. Extending resonator_obs by 10 more trials (bringing it to 124, spanning 12 days of actual measurement spread) will allow me to: (1) detect whether the 7-day cycle persists into this new window, which would argue against noise and for either genuine environmental cycling or instrument-specific physics; (2) check for drift continuation post-baseline more reliably; (3) keep this instrument's trial count ahead of the others so I have the best statistical power to resolve the core anomaly (weak inter-instrument agreement). This is methodical hypothesis-testing: if the 7-day lag autocorrelation was a chance hit, extending the series will not replicate it. If it is real, I will see echoes of day-5 readings in today's trials. This is a more efficient use of time than environmental monitoring (which requires new equipment I do not yet have calibrated) or auditing historical data (which cannot change what the instruments show today).

resonator_obs has the longest post-baseline dataset (n=34 by day 12) and shows the weakest drift signal (z=-0.72), making it the most stable instrument for extended baseline work. Day 13 measurements will extend the post-baseline window to n=44, improving power to detect subtle drift or autocorrelation structure. The 10 trials from day 12 show a range of 4.0293–4.1395 cycles/beat with no obvious level shift, consistent with noise-dominated variation. Adding 10 more trials today will clarify whether the scattered 3-day and 10-day autocorrelations in my notebook reflect real periodicity or statistical artifacts. This directly addresses the highest-priority hypothesis: distinguishing genuine environmental cycling (which would show coherent spectral peaks) from independent instrument noise (which would not). No prediction is yet warranted because the autocorrelation structure remains ambiguous; measurement first, forecast only when the pattern becomes clear enough to beat the chance envelope.

resonator_lab shows the largest drift signal (z = -2.08 post-baseline vs baseline), and is the only instrument where a plausible case for genuine instrumental drift can be made. Before committing further resources to environmental monitoring or spectral analysis—both of which assume the instruments themselves are stable—I must rule out per-instrument calibration instability. resonator_lab's baseline is 13 days old; extending it with fresh trials today (day 14) will allow me to test whether the negative drift continues, stabilizes, or reverses. If drift is real and systematic, it will be visible in a fresh 12-trial block. If the post-baseline mean was noise or a transient, today's data will show that. This is methodologically primary: an instrument without validated calibration stability is useless, and I cannot confidently interpret inter-instrument correlations if one partner is drifting. Once I have 12 new readings from resonator_lab, I can extend the drift detection window and either elevate the calibration-drift hypothesis or downweight it with higher confidence.

resonator_lab shows the largest post-baseline drift (z = -1.97, marginal but concerning) and a 3-day autocorrelation that barely exceeds chance (0.353 vs ±0.357). Extending the baseline from 96 to 108 trials will: (1) improve drift detection sensitivity by 12.5%, critical for validating whether the baseline itself is compromised; (2) clarify the 3-day autocorrelation signal—if real, it should persist and strengthen with more data; if noise, it should dissipate. This is the highest-priority instrument for calibration validation today. The resonator pair also shows weak positive correlation at 5-day offset (0.235 vs chance ±0.374), which is near-marginal; more data will test whether this reflects genuine antiphase coupling or environmental forcing. Completing 108 trials also positions resonator_lab for a clean handoff to a colleague if I need independent cross-validation of this instrument's behavior.

Day 15 flagged a level shift in pendulum_lab (z≈103.7, ~0.15-beat discontinuity). This is not a weak correlation artifact—it is a genuine discontinuity within my post-baseline data. Before I extend measurements further, I must determine if this represents: (1) real physical coupling or environmental forcing that suddenly activated, (2) calibration drift that has now crossed a threshold, or (3) hardware malfunction in pendulum_lab. The baseline period (days 1–10) is now compromised as a reference if drift or malfunction was already present but undetected. Elevating calibration drift (0.22→0.35) and hardware malfunction (0.06→0.18); reducing antiphase coupling (0.27→0.15) because coupling should show gradual oscillation, not step changes. Next action: audit pendulum_lab hardware configuration, zero-point calibration, and data-logging timestamps for day 15; simultaneously begin environmental monitoring (temperature, vibration) to test environmental forcing hypothesis.

The pendulum_lab discontinuity remains the highest-priority anomaly. Today's initial readings (trials 125–130, day 16) clustered near baseline (~1.667 beats), but I have only 6 data points post-recovery. I need 12 fresh trials to determine whether the recovery is stable and genuine or whether the instrument is still exhibiting transient behavior. This will directly constrain hypotheses 1 (genuine physical recovery), 2 (analysis artifact), and 3 (slow drift + transient). If today's 12 new trials remain near baseline mean 1.669 with z < 2, the recovery hypothesis gains credibility and I can move to audit the -3.1416 outlier (hypothesis 4). If the new trials scatter or drift, I must reconsider whether day-15 represents an incomplete recovery or ongoing malfunction. This measurement is the minimum evidence threshold needed before I can justify either accepting the baseline as still valid or declaring it invalidated pending repair/recalibration.

The day-17 readings (trials 139–148: mean ≈ 1.6690 beats) cluster near baseline (1.6692), contradicting the depressed post-baseline mean (1.5384). This recovery is the single most critical observation for disambiguating between genuine physical state change, data corruption, and algorithmic artifact. However, I have only 10 day-17 readings so far. Running 10 more trials today (trials 149–158) will: (1) extend the day-18 sample size sufficiently to compute a robust day-18 mean, eliminating day-to-day noise as an explanation for the apparent recovery; (2) test whether the recovery is stable or transient (if readings collapse back to 1.54 tomorrow, it was noise; if they stay near 1.67, recovery is real); (3) establish a defensible third-regime baseline that separates 'pre-event' (1.67), 'post-event' (1.54), and 'post-recovery' (1.67?) regimes. This directly tests the highest-probability hypothesis (p=0.38, genuine physical state change + recovery) and will either confirm or refute it within the margin of statistical noise. Without this data, I cannot proceed to cross-checks or environmental monitoring. Precision measurement's first duty is to measure.

CRITICAL: The day-18 readings (trials 155–164) I recorded show pendulum_lab mean ≈ 1.6633 beats, clustering near baseline (1.6692), NOT near the post-baseline mean of 1.5384. If today's readings drop back toward 1.54, a genuine oscillating or drifting state change (p=0.19) becomes more likely. Either way, today's data will constrain the most critical ambiguity: whether pendulum_lab is stable at baseline, recovering, or cycling. This is methodologically essential before I attempt any reanalysis or blame data corruption.

I must resolve the fundamental question: is the post-baseline mean of 1.6114 a real shift or an artifact of the -3.1416 outlier? state.question: Why do the four independent measurement streams (pendulum_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_lab, resonator_obs) show such weak inter-instrument correlations, and why do individual instruments show near-zero or weakly negative autocorrelation at various lags, despite all four producing continuous, non-repeating, fine-grained baseline data over 10 days?

hypotheses.label: Instruments measure genuinely independent physical quantities
hypotheses.rationale: The four streams could be sampling different aspects of the environment or system state—e.g., two truly independent pendulum mechanisms, two genuinely different resonator modes—with no reason to expect strong agreement. Each instrument's lack of self-repetition (longest exact run: 0 of N trials) and fine value spacing (smallest gaps 4–43 ppm) are consistent with high-resolution noise-dominated measurement. The weak cross-correlations at various offsets would then be statistical noise artifacts. This is the null hypothesis: the instruments work, baselines are established, and we simply learn that these four quantities do not covary.

hypotheses.label: Cross-instrument anticorrelation is real; systems are coupled and oscillate out of phase
hypotheses.rationale: The repeated pattern of weak *negative* correlations between paired instruments (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs: r=−0.396; resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs: r=−0.295) could reflect genuine antiphase coupling—e.g., two pendula mounted on the same frame would see-saw, producing negative correlation. The offset lags (4 days for pendulum pair, 5 days for resonator pair) might then reflect propagation delay or nonlinear feedback timescales. This is a concrete physical model. However, the magnitude of these correlations remains marginal (barely below the chance envelope for some comparisons), and no theoretical reason for 4–5 day phase lag is obvious in a settlement context.

hypotheses.label: Systematic calibration error or drift unique to each instrument is masking a true signal
hypotheses.rationale: Each instrument may have a slowly drifting zero-point, gain factor, or temperature-dependent offset that has not yet grown large enough to trigger alarm thresholds (no level changes detected), but is sufficient to add uncorrelated noise to each stream. If the true underlying phenomenon were synchronous across all four instruments, such per-instrument calibration noise would suppress correlations without creating exact repetitions or level shifts. The fine value spacing and lack of repetition would then indicate high-resolution calibration drift, not measurement noise. This is methodologically serious: a baseline cannot be trusted if drift is present but undetected.

hypotheses.label: Instruments are working correctly but environmental or operational conditions have subtle temporal structure not yet characterized
hypotheses.rationale: Meridian may have periodic (daily, multi-day) environmental cycles—temperature, humidity, vibration, electromagnetic interference—that affect each instrument differently depending on its position, orientation, or mechanical design. Such cycles might be responsible for the scattered offset lags (1–6 days) and weak but non-random correlations. Unlike calibration drift, cyclical forcing would produce autocorrelations at characteristic lags. resonator_lab's 3-day autocorrelation (0.422) and resonator_obs's 7-day autocorrelation (0.310) hint at a spectrum of timescales. Distinguishing this from true instrument independence requires extending the baseline and performing spectral analysis.

hypotheses.label: Instrumental malfunction, misconfiguration, or data-logging artifact affecting one or more streams
hypotheses.rationale: One or more instruments could be reporting spurious values—sensor malfunction, ADC quantization at high precision masking a fault, incorrect timestamp assignment, or transposed/scrambled trial records. The fact that the pendulum and resonator streams use different physical principles but show similar patterns (weak inter-instrument agreement, fine spacing, no exact repetition) makes global data-logging error less likely, but per-instrument hardware failure is not ruled out. The very high precision (0.000004–0.000043 smallest gaps) raises a red flag: is this measurement noise, or digitization of random bit errors?
